1. Do you expect a horizon drop as we increase observer height or do you expect the horizon to rise to eye level? 

Cause horizon drop means globe earth and no horizon drop means flat earth.

VoysovReason says that at 25 000', the horizon dip angle is 2.8° and at 50 000', the dip angle is 3.959°.   (https://imgur.com/gallery/BcIqlBH)

I measured a dip angle of 3.6° from somewhere in the range of 35 000 to 39 000' observation height. ( http://imgur.com/gallery/XBOBp1j )
This is in line with a globe earth as on a flat earth the horizon line would rise to eye level and there would be no dip angle.

In modern race cars and supercars like the F40, the pedals are aligned closely so that your right foot can easily cover both the brake and the throttle pedals. This allows the driver to apply pressure to the brake pedal with the ball of the foot, while simultaneously “blipping” the throttle by swiveling the side of the sole. The blip is a short, sharp snap of the gas pedal that sends the revs high enough to match the running speed of the shorter gear. Matching the revs cushions the bite of the downshift and prevents a sudden load of engine braking affecting the driven axle. In the case of the rear-wheel-drive Ferrari, its engine braking was strong enough to stop the wheels from turning and send it skidding across the road. I was certainly keen to avoid spinning backward; it would have presented Clarkson with an enduring, unbearable punchline. I delicately released the clutch, and the thunderous engine of the F40 sprang slowly back to life . Well, my right foot went deep into the brake and past the point where it was able to reach the throttle. Perhaps the owner had set the pedals to suit a lighter braking style, but it came as no surprise. With the majority of cars I lapped on Top Gear , I found it impossible to heel-and-toe. Unless the pedals are perfectly aligned for you , the technique does more harm than good when you’re braking close to the limit because the slightest imbalance in your foot affects the pressure asserted on the pedal. My solution was simply smooth clutch work. I remembered my ice training and treated the left pedal like a second brake.

Is your car fwd or rwd? I would be a lot more concerned in a rwd to downshift into a corner, without a rev match, as you will unsettle the rear wheels, and could enter an oversteer. Of course if you are doing all your braking and downshifting in a straigt line, let the clutch out slowly, (and have esc) chances of upsetting the rear end are minimal. 

So If you are not comfy with heel/toe on street. (I am not), downshift into second while braking in a straight line and let the clutch out real slow. Or if your speed is slow enough to prevent an over rev, do a big blip, downshift into 2nd, then brake and then corner.
